newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan-Russia islands talks have much at stake.
newsitem.headline: Japan-Russia islands talks have much at stake.

text.p: Japan walks a delicate line in talks with Russia this week over a long-running islands dispute because even progress on the issue could rekindle similiar rows with South Korea and China.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov arrives in Tokyo on Thursday and holds a full day of talks on Friday with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto. He departs on Sunday.

The dispute over the islands, called the Southern Kuriles by Moscow and Northern Territories by Tokyo, has prevented them from formally signing a World War Two peace treaty. The islands were seized by the advancing Red Army in 1945.
Government sources said any concessions on the part of Japan this time might be interpreted by South Korea and China as a signal to go on the offensive over their own islands disputes with Japan,
"One mistake this round (with Russia) and we might invite gross misunderstandings from South Korea and China," one senior government official said.

The row over the Japanese-named Senkaku Islands in the East China Sea, called Diaoyu Islands and claimed by both Taiwan and China, flared up in September when a pro-Chinese Hong Kong activist drowned during a protest near the islands.
China and Taiwan were especially incensed at the construction of a make-shift lighthouse on one of the islands by a Japanese ultra-nationalist group earlier this year.

South Koreans also held anti-Japanese protests earlier this year when Japan repeated its claim to Korea-held Tokdo island in the Sea of Japan, called Takeshima by Tokyo. South Korea has stationed border troops there.

Japan's talks with Primakov this time are especially sensitive because he might formally propose a joint development plan for the Northern Territories/Southern Kuriles after setting aside the question of sovereignty, officials said.
"In the past the Russian side has hinted at this sort of plan but they have never given us any details," Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said on Tuesday.
"Japan is ready to listen to such a proposal, so long as it does not damage Japan's fundamental claim to the islands," Hashimoto told a news conference.

Such an arrangement would follow a similar scheme adopted by Britain and Argentina over the Falkland Islands, which Buenos Aires calls the Malvinas. The two countries went to war over the South Atlantic islands in 1982.
In 1993 during President Boris Yeltsin's visit to Tokyo, Russia did agree in a joint communique that the dispute itself existed, a half-step forward from the Cold War era.
Until then the Kremlin stood fast by its claim that there was no dispute at all with Japan.
